clue.text: Local tender I'd backed with severe criticism about separate points

indicators.note: something backed has been sent the other way, so its letters run in reverse
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes around others

blocks.note: I'd written without the apostrophe
a stricture is a sharp critical remark
two compass points, north and south, slotted in at different places

explanation.surface: A council's local tender, retracted after harsh criticism over a few disputed points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like a contract bid but is one who tends the sick. 'Separate' tells you the two compass points do not go in side by side but at different places.
explanation.definitionFit: A British community nurse visits patients at home within an assigned area, so she is a carer attached to one locality.

clue.text: Pottery like C. Rossetti's 22 and water at Christmas

blocks.note: 22 is EARTH; in her carol 'In the Bleak Midwinter' the earth stood hard as iron
the same carol has water like a stone

explanation.surface: Some earthenware is compared with lines from a Christmas poem about frozen ground and water.
explanation.walkthrough: Christina Rossetti's carol 'In the Bleak Midwinter' says 'Earth stood hard as iron, water like a stone'; the cross-reference to 22 supplies the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironstone china is a hard, durable white earthenware first made in Staffordshire, a kind of ceramic ware.

clue.text: Devil said as expected what wasn't said

blocks.note: an imp is a little devil
a devil, true to type, speaks falsely

explanation.surface: A devil predictably saying something, set against something left unsaid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said as expected' only works with the devil before it: what anyone expects a devil to do when speaking is to tell untruths.
explanation.definitionFit: Something implied is suggested or hinted at without being stated outright, so it was never put into words.

clue.text: So sorry (odds when backed included) it was in god's hand

indicators.note: the odd-numbered positions of a word, first, third and fifth, are kept
backed means sent backwards, so the kept letters run in reverse
something included is taken inside, so these letters go within the other piece

blocks.note: thus means so, in that way
first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: An apology with an aside about betting odds, then something held by a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So sorry' reads as one apology, but 'So' is a separate word for THUS and 'sorry' only lends its odd letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A thyrsus is the ivy-wreathed staff topped with a pine cone carried by Dionysus (Bacchus) and his followers.

clue.text: River Lune produce gets cut (past tense)

definitions.note: punning: a past-participle form that means tense

indicators.note: to produce is to make something new out of material, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river
taken as written; the Lune is a river in north-west England
axed means cut, as of jobs or budgets

explanation.surface: Goods from a Lancashire river are cut back, with a grammar note added in brackets.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like a grammar label, but it is the definition: a word ending in -ED, so a past form, that means tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrelaxed means stiff, strained or anxious, exactly what tense describes, and its -ed ending makes it look like a past form.

clue.text: You've kept us waiting: it's the turn of Rome to benefit

indicators.note: a turn is a twist or rotation, so the following letters are spun into a new order

blocks.note: all thirteen letters used as they stand

explanation.surface: An impatient complaint, then a claim that Rome's moment for gain has finally come round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' reads as Rome's turn, as in taking turns, but it is the instruction to rearrange the thirteen letters that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something came not before time is a wry remark that it arrived late, which is what a person grumbles after a long wait.

clue.text: Test for doctor at island on lake

blocks.note: an intern is a junior hospital doctor
taken as written
Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A medical exam for a doctor, held on an island in a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test' looks like a medical exam but means a Test match; 'on' places the lake after the island in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A Test is a full cricket or rugby match between national sides, which is also called an international.

clue.text: Description of high spots as fantastic orgy with Oprah

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful or bizarre, so the letters take an unexpected new shape

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone recounts the highlights of a wild party with a famous talk-show host.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High spots' suggests highlights of an evening, but it means literally high places, mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: Orography is the branch of physical geography that describes and maps mountains and their relief.

clue.text: Bird to be hungry?

blocks.note: first meaning: a large black crow
second meaning: an old verb meaning to feed or crave greedily

explanation.walkthrough: The verb survives mostly in the adjective ravenous; the bird and the verb are unrelated words that happen to share a spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a big black corvid, and the archaic verb means to devour or hunt for food voraciously.

clue.text: In the meantime, apply fat

blocks.note: first meaning: to tack fabric with long loose stitches that hold it only until the final sewing
second meaning: to moisten roasting meat with its juices

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a playful hint rather than a synonym: basting stitches are temporary, there only for the meantime.
explanation.definitionFit: In sewing it means tacking loosely as a stopgap, and in cookery it means spooning dripping or butter over a roast.

clue.text: Cheek only found in pub and church

indicators.note: what is found in a place lies inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: sole means only, single
an inn is a pub
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A complaint that rudeness turns up only at the pub and in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found in pub and church' reads as two places where cheek turns up, but only the pub holds the other piece; the church simply follows. CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheek is impudent, disrespectful talk or behaviour, and insolence is the formal word for such rudeness.

clue.text: Highwayman's measure for paper?

blocks.note: a foot is a unit of length
a pad is a block of writing paper

explanation.surface: A question about what unit a highwayman would use to measure paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'measure for paper' is being read as a unit plus a writing block.
explanation.definitionFit: A footpad was a robber who attacked travellers on foot, the unmounted counterpart of the mounted road robber.

clue.text: I sold birds from river last month at Queens

blocks.note: the Po is Italy's longest river
ult., short for ultimo, means of last month in old business letters
ER (Elizabeth Regina) twice, one for each queen

explanation.surface: A trader recalls selling birds from beside a river last month, at a place called Queens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queens' looks like the New York borough, but it is two lots of ER, the royal cipher for a queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A poulterer is a dealer in chickens, ducks and game, so 'I sold birds' is that trader speaking in the first person.

clue.text: Tombstone writer finds no point in a three-pipe problem

indicators.note: having no point means losing a compass letter, so one is taken away
a problem is a tangle to be worked out, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
one E, east, is dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sherlock Holmes called a puzzling case 'a three-pipe problem'; here a gravestone writer stumbles on one.
explanation.walkthrough: The Holmes allusion is a decoy: 'a three-pipe' loses one E (east, a compass point) and the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitapher composes epitaphs, the memorial inscriptions carved on graves and monuments.

clue.text: Painter to tolerate returning vessel

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to bear is to put up with
an urn is a vase-like vessel

explanation.surface: An artist must put up with a ship coming back to port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship, but it is a container, the kind for ashes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry Raeburn was the leading Scottish portrait artist of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

clue.text: 12's agreement retaining other number's agreement

indicators.note: the other way round means reversed, so these letters are flipped
to retain is to hold on to, so one piece keeps another inside it

blocks.note: a nod signals agreement
No. is the abbreviation for number
ay (aye) means yes

explanation.surface: A grammatical puzzle about one number agreeing with another.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' is not the cross-reference to 12 across but the hour, twelve o'clock. 'Agreement' appears twice with two different answers, a nod and the old word aye.
explanation.definitionFit: Noonday is midday, twelve o'clock in the middle of the day, when the sun is highest.

clue.text: Hand about to append a particular person

indicators.note: to be about something is to go around it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: a fist is a clenched hand
to add is to append

explanation.surface: An instruction to put a handwritten addition on a document naming a specific person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A particular person' sounds like 'a specific individual', but particular here means fussy.
explanation.definitionFit: A faddist follows food or health crazes and is fussy about what they will accept, so particular in the choosy sense.

clue.text: Slip maybe by churchman providing backing at first

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word is read in reverse

blocks.note: providing means if, on condition that
an elder is an officer of a Presbyterian church

explanation.surface: A clergyman's mistake, perhaps, made while he was giving support to someone at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slip' wants to be an error, but in cricket a slip is a catching position beside the wicketkeeper, and whoever stands there is one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Slip is one of the cricket positions taken by a player on the fielding side, so a slip is one example of that player.

clue.text: Land of the Arthurian legends

indicators.note: made of means formed out of part of, so the letters come from inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the end of one word and the start of the next
surface padding that completes the phrase and gives no letters

explanation.surface: A phrase naming the realm of King Arthur's tales, such as Camelot.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue invites you to name a legendary kingdom, but the letters sit across the join of 'the' and 'Arthurian'.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth can mean dry ground or soil as opposed to sea, which is the sense of land here.

clue.text: Thinker about love will nearly front the gallery

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the end of a word is cut off

blocks.note: to front an audience is to play to the gallery; the gallery itself gives no letters

explanation.surface: A philosopher of love who will almost always court the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: To play to the gallery is to show off for popular approval; PLAY loses its last letter and TO stays.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek philosopher wrote the Symposium on love, and 'Platonic love' carries his name to this day.

clue.text: Supergrass?

blocks.note: surface reading: British slang for a criminal who informs on many associates
setter's reading: split in two, a super thing that also grasses, since the fruit is slang for anything excellent and an old verb means to inform

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the one word should be broken in half: something super and something that grasses, with one word covering both.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit is slang for anything outstanding, and the same word is an old verb meaning to betray or tell tales on accomplices.

clue.text: Bond missing junction on the road to the Isles

definitions.text: on the road to the Isles

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: mortar bonds bricks together
a T-junction, shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: A link is lost at a crossroads on the route to the Scottish islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Road to the Isles' is a Scottish song whose singer heads by Tummel, Loch Rannoch and Lochaber towards the Hebrides; Morar is on that route, the West Highland road to Mallaig.
explanation.definitionFit: Morar is a village and loch in the western Highlands, passed on the way to the ferry for Skye and the Hebrides.

clue.text: Coin tricked wicked landlord who shall be nameless

indicators.note: staying nameless means dropping the name, so its abbreviation is struck out

blocks.note: to do someone is to cheat them
Peter Rachman, a notorious slum landlord in 1950s London; N for name is then lost

explanation.surface: A coin was used to trick a cruel landlord whose identity must stay secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Who shall be nameless' is the usual coy phrase for avoiding naming someone; here it removes N, the abbreviation for name.
explanation.definitionFit: A didrachma was an ancient Greek silver piece worth two drachmas, so a unit of currency.

clue.text: Clamour about "The Lady Killer", tough drama

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a cry is a loud outcry
her refers to a lady
the orc or orca is the killer whale
hard means tough

explanation.surface: An outcry over a film called 'The Ladykiller', described as a tough piece of theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Lady Killer' looks like one title, but it splits into the lady and the killer whale.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The Cherry Orchard' is Chekhov's last play, a classic of the Russian stage first performed in 1904.
